title: MCP servers can now teach Claude how to do a job, run long tasks and ask before risky steps. Anthropic’s agents moved its API to Rust after tests hid most real-world differences, and GitHub will bill Copilot code review to organisations from 30 December. The UK’s FCA sets rules for AI agents in finance, 42 states fight Character.AI’s chat auction, the New York Times pauses Photoshop 2027, and GPT-6.2 designs proteins that bind in the lab.
summary: Anthropic put Skills over MCP into public beta and made Tasks and Elicitation generally available, so connectors can ship playbooks, run background jobs and pause for approval. Its Messages API now runs on Rust with about 70% less CPU per request, after Claude agents fixed differences that tests missed: about 98% of tests passed in April but only about a quarter of live inputs matched. GitHub will bill unset Copilot code review to organisations from 30 December. The FCA says firms stay responsible for agents and tech firms may need authorisation. 42 attorneys general oppose the 1 December sale of chats from more than 21 million Character.AI accounts. The New York Times told freelancers to avoid Photoshop 2027 over AI tags, and OpenAI says 35 of 322 GPT-6.2-designed minibinders bound their targets.
uncertainty: Skills over MCP is a beta and reaches Enterprise later. Anthropic’s Rust figures are its own and its CPU figure covers one region. GitHub’s change applies only where no billing choice is saved. The FCA page sets expectations, not new rules. The Character.AI sale depends on the bankruptcy court. The Times has not said which Photoshop features it means, and Adobe had not responded. OpenAI’s protein results are a preprint, used specialised models to supply sequences and pick candidates, and have not been independently replicated.

stories.theme: MCP servers can now ship skills, run long jobs in the background, and stop to ask you before risky steps in Claude
stories.changed: On 24 November 2026, two years after it launched the Model Context Protocol (MCP), Anthropic added three things to how Claude works with MCP servers, the connectors that link it to other apps. Skills over MCP, in public beta, lets a server publish skills alongside its tools: written playbooks for how to do a job, such as step-by-step workflows or rules tailored to your account. Claude loads a skill only when it needs it, and skills update with the server, so there is nothing separate to install. Shopify uses it to help Claude design and update a merchant’s store end to end, HubSpot to onboard customers, and Atlassian to draw on company context; Carta will use it to draft and issue equity from an uploaded document. Tasks, now generally available, lets a server run a long job, or a whole agent loop, in the background while Claude keeps working and collects the result later; ZoomInfo uses it for deeper account and contact research. Elicitation, also generally available, lets a server pause and ask you for input or approval through a form or link: Supabase confirms costs before creating a paid project and before destructive SQL, Railway asks before removing a service, and GitHub makes you type a repository’s name before an agent deletes it. File Uploads, which sends PDFs, spreadsheets and images straight to a server, is coming soon. Anthropic says MCP has over 700 million monthly SDK downloads and over 10,000 connectors for Claude.
stories.matters: Until now a connector told Claude what it could do, not how to do it well, and every tool call had to finish before Claude moved on. Skills put the vendor’s know-how inside the connector, and Elicitation builds an “are you sure?” step into the tool itself rather than leaving it to the model.
stories.imply: The apps you connect will start to behave more like trained colleagues than bare buttons. For admins, the questions shift from “which connectors are allowed?” to “whose playbooks is Claude following, and which actions ask a person first?”
uses: Check which of your Claude connectors (Shopify, HubSpot, Atlassian, GitHub, Supabase) now ship skills, and try one end-to-end job instead of single commands.
Hand a slow research or reporting job to a connector that supports Tasks, and keep working in the same chat.
If you build an MCP server, add Elicitation before anything that spends money or deletes data.
stories.example: A small online shop owner asks Claude to refresh the winter collection page. Shopify’s skill walks Claude through the store’s theme and product rules, and before anything is published, a form asks the owner to approve the changes.
stories.audience: People who use Claude with business apps, developers who build MCP servers, and Team admins, who must switch Skills over MCP on.
stories.watch: Skills over MCP is on by default for Pro, Max and Ultra, needs an admin on Team plans and is coming soon to Enterprise. Tasks and Elicitation are rolling out to Team and Enterprise. Watch whether other AI apps adopt the same open extensions.

source.title: Claude by Anthropic: MCP servers can now ship skills, run tasks, and more with Claude, 24 November 2026
source.quote: With Skills over MCP, servers can publish skills alongside their tools to help Claude take on longer, multi-step work.

stories.theme: Anthropic used teams of Claude agents to move its main API from Python to Rust, and found passing tests was not enough
stories.changed: On 25 November 2026 Anthropic described how it moved its Messages API, the service customers and its own apps such as Claude Code use to reach Claude, from Python to Rust. API traffic grew roughly 1,800 times from early 2024 to fall 2026, and Rust uses far less computing power per request. Claude wrote a first version of the core request path in about a week. The hard part was proving the new version behaved like the old one. In April the Rust API passed about 98% of its tests, yet only about a quarter of inputs matched the Python API on real production traffic, because live requests hit cases the roughly 700 integration tests did not cover. So the team ran live requests through both versions, compared each step, and grouped differences by a “fingerprint”. A coordinating Claude agent assigned a worker agent to each new kind of difference; the agent reproduced it, fixed the Rust code and posted the fix and evidence in Slack for engineers to review. Corrections were saved as rules every later agent could read. Public traffic moved to Rust in September. The result, Anthropic says: about 70% less CPU per request and about 20% shorter median time to first token, without taking the service offline or freezing feature work.
stories.matters: This is a detailed account of AI agents rebuilding a live, business-critical system, not a demo. Its main lesson is about checking: a near-perfect test score hid that three in four real requests came out different.
stories.imply: If you let agents rewrite or migrate systems, budget most of the effort for proving the new version matches the old one on real work. People’s role moves to deciding what counts as correct and reviewing fixes, not typing the code.
uses: Before trusting an agent-written replacement, run real (anonymised) inputs through old and new versions and compare the outputs.
Group differences by pattern so one bug is fixed once, not hundreds of times.
Keep a shared rules file where reviewers’ corrections are written down for the next agent.
stories.example: A finance team lets an agent rebuild its invoice-matching script. Instead of stopping at the tests, they run last month’s invoices through both versions and find 40 that come out differently, all from one date-format rule.
stories.audience: Engineering leads, platform teams and anyone planning an AI-assisted migration of a system other people depend on.
stories.watch: Whether other companies publish similar numbers for agent-led migrations, and how much human review time such projects really need.

source.title: Anthropic: Migrating our Messages API to Rust, 25 November 2026
source.quote: Our Rust API passed about 98% of its tests in April, yet only about a quarter of inputs matched on production traffic

stories.theme: GitHub will bill Copilot code reviews to the organisation from 30 December unless admins choose otherwise
stories.changed: On 25 November 2026 GitHub said that, for organisations and enterprises on Copilot Business or Copilot Enterprise that have not chosen how to bill Copilot code review, reviews by members with a paid Copilot licence will be billed to the organisation that owns the repository from 30 December 2026. Today, when no choice is saved, those reviews use the member’s own Copilot entitlement. Organisations that already picked Member or Organization keep their choice, and the separate setting for members without a Copilot licence does not change. Accounts without AI Credits paid usage, with a billing lock or with no billable customer will be set to Member instead. To keep things as they are, an admin selects Member in the organisation or enterprise Copilot policy settings before 30 December; where an enterprise manages the setting, an enterprise owner makes the choice. Until then, unset settings show Default (Member) with a notice.
stories.matters: AI code review runs on every pull request, so who pays adds up fast. A default that quietly moves the bill from personal allowances to the company account is the kind of change finance only notices when the invoice arrives.
stories.imply: AI tools are moving from per-seat prices to metered usage charged to the organisation. Someone in each company needs to own these settings, the same way someone owns cloud budgets.
uses: Open your organisation’s Copilot policy settings this week and check what code review billing shows.
Decide deliberately: Member keeps costs inside licences; Organization may suit teams that want reviews on every repo.
If you choose Organization, set a spending alert on AI Credits paid usage.
stories.example: An engineering manager at a 60-person startup sees “Default (Member)” in the Copilot settings, agrees with finance to keep member billing for now, and selects Member before the holidays so January’s bill holds no surprise.
stories.audience: GitHub organisation and enterprise admins, engineering managers and finance teams paying for Copilot Business or Enterprise.
stories.watch: 30 December 2026, when the default changes, and whether other AI coding tools move review costs to company accounts too.

source.title: GitHub Changelog: Copilot code review billing will default to the organization, 25 November 2026
source.quote: Organization billing requires AI Credits paid usage and can increase your organization’s spending.

stories.theme: The UK’s financial regulator says firms stay responsible for the AI agents they use, and tech firms whose agents move money may need its permission
stories.changed: On 24 November 2026 the UK’s Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) published its approach to agentic AI, meaning AI that can act, not just answer, in financial services. For regulated firms, responsibility for following the rules stays with the firm and its senior managers even when the agent comes from a third party; firms must show they understand the systems they use, how much freedom those systems have, the risks and the controls needed in real time and under stress. Firms should also plan for customers who send AI agents to deal with them: how to tell they are dealing with an agent, what consent is in place, what the agent may do, how customers get help when something goes wrong, and whether to accept payments instructed by an agent or from a wallet an agent controls. For technology providers and social media platforms, the FCA says calling yourself a tech company does not settle whether you need authorisation: an agent that handles payments, gives financial advice, arranges credit or issues financial promotions may be doing regulated work. The FCA says it will intervene against unauthorised financial services, expects clear disclaimers about the limits of AI financial information, and plans an Agentic Policy Sprint for firms and tech providers.
stories.matters: Shopping and assistant agents are starting to pay, borrow and invest for people. The UK regulator is saying the old rules apply to them, and that the company behind an agent cannot hide behind the word “technology”.
stories.imply: Banks, insurers and fintechs need a plan for agent customers, not just their own AI. AI companies launching money features in the UK should expect to talk to the FCA early.
uses: Risk and compliance teams: list where AI agents act for your firm and who the accountable senior manager is for each.
Customer teams: decide how you will recognise and handle an AI agent calling or messaging on a customer’s behalf.
Product teams at AI companies: check whether a planned payment or advice feature could count as regulated activity.
stories.example: A UK building society gets a mortgage enquiry sent by a customer’s AI assistant. Its new process checks the customer has authorised the agent, limits the agent to fetching information, and sends any application to the customer to sign.
stories.audience: Compliance and risk teams at UK financial firms, fintech founders, and AI companies offering agents to UK consumers.
stories.watch: The FCA’s regular updates on the same page, the Agentic Policy Sprint, and any first action against an unauthorised agent product.

source.title: Financial Conduct Authority: Our approach to Agentic AI, 24 November 2026
source.quote: Just because a business describes itself as a technology provider does not mean that they do not need to be authorised by us to provide financial services in the UK.

stories.theme: Bankrupt Character.AI plans to auction millions of users’ private chats, and 42 US attorneys general ask the court to stop it
stories.changed: On 24 November 2026 California Attorney General Rob Bonta said he had joined a bipartisan coalition of 42 attorneys general opposing Character.AI’s plan to sell its platform and the private chat histories of more than 21 million US accounts, more than 2.1 million of them registered to minors, at an auction set for 1 December 2026. The sale would include users’ personal data such as IP addresses and other metadata, and risk scores the company gave users. Character.AI filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in October and had told users it does not sell personal information. The states say the deal places no duties on the buyer: it would not have to follow Character.AI’s privacy policy or honour opt-out and deletion requests, and could pass the data on. The only bidder named so far, Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC, was set up in Delaware on 13 November, one day before Character.AI picked it as the opening bid. The states ask the court to reject the sale terms, the bidder and its proposed $350,000 break-up fee, and at a minimum to leave out children’s chats and other sensitive data. TechCrunch reported the story on 25 November.
stories.matters: People tell chatbots things they tell no one else. This case tests whether those conversations become just another asset to sell when an AI company fails.
stories.imply: A privacy promise is only as strong as what happens in bankruptcy. Before staff or customers pour sensitive details into any AI service, ask what happens to the data if the company is sold or goes under.
uses: If you or your children used Character.AI, check its settings and consider deleting chats before 1 December.
In vendor reviews, ask AI suppliers what their contracts say about data in a sale or bankruptcy.
Remind staff not to put personal or client details into consumer chatbots.
stories.example: A school counsellor who once suggested a “study buddy” bot to students sends parents a short note about the auction and how to delete chats.
stories.audience: Parents, privacy and procurement teams, and anyone who has shared personal matters with an AI companion app.
stories.watch: The bankruptcy court’s ruling before or at the 1 December auction, and new chatbot safety laws in California, Colorado, New York and Connecticut that take effect on 1 January 2027.

source.title: California Department of Justice: Attorney General Bonta Opposes Asset Sale of Character.AI Amid Child Safety Concerns, 24 November 2026
source.quote: This kind of behavior is illegal under federal and California law and bankruptcy should not be used to sidestep these consumer protections

stories.theme: The New York Times tells freelance photographers not to use Photoshop 2027, because its hidden AI features can label photos as AI-edited
stories.changed: The New York Times has told freelance photographers not to use the newest version of Adobe Photoshop when working for it, The Verge reported on 24 November 2026. In an email from photography leaders Meaghan Looram and Josh Haner, the Times says features in the 2027 update use AI “in ways that may not be apparent to users” and “can result in metadata identifying photographs as AI-generated.” The rule covers Photoshop 2027, release 28.0.0 and later updates; a Times spokesperson confirmed it. The November update adds an AI Assisted Editor view, an AI assistant for step-by-step editing, prompt-based editing, new AI upscaling and a tool that recomposes images for new canvas sizes. Since August Adobe has been adding C2PA content credentials, tags that record whether an image was made or edited with AI, across its apps. The Times has said it does not retouch or digitally manipulate photos beyond minimal colour adjustments, so an AI tag on a news photo could cost readers’ trust. It is not yet clear which features the Times means, and Adobe had not answered The Verge.
stories.matters: AI is now built so deeply into everyday tools that people can use it without knowing, and the labels meant to build trust can then mislead. A major newsroom is choosing to freeze its software rather than risk that.
stories.imply: Any team that promises “no AI” in its work, from newsrooms to legal and medical imaging, needs to know which features in its tools count as AI and what tags they leave behind.
uses: Photo, design and comms teams: check which Photoshop version freelancers and staff use for work with strict authenticity rules.
Open a sample exported file in a content credentials viewer to see what it says about AI.
Write down which editing tools are allowed for work you label as unedited.
stories.example: A charity’s comms lead learns a campaign photo carries an AI-edited tag only because an automatic selection tool was used, and sets a rule that documentary photos are edited in an older, approved version.
stories.audience: Photographers, picture editors, comms and marketing teams, and anyone whose work depends on proving an image is real.
stories.watch: Adobe’s answer on which features add AI tags, and whether other news organisations or agencies follow the Times.

source.title: The Verge: The New York Times warns photographers not to update Photoshop over AI features, 24 November 2026
source.quote: At this time, we are requiring that all contributing photographers avoid using Adobe Photoshop 2027 (release 28.0.0 and subsequent updates) when working on assignment for The Times

stories.theme: OpenAI says GPT-6 models can design proteins with reasoning and code alone, and some designs bound their targets in the lab
stories.changed: On 24 November 2026 OpenAI published a preprint saying its GPT-6 models can design new protein shapes and sequences using only reasoning and general-purpose code, without calling specialised biology models to generate them. With research partner Onava it tested designs in the lab. A pre-release version of GPT-6.2 designed three-dimensional shapes for minibinders, small proteins meant to attach to a chosen target, for five targets; a specialised model called SolubleMPNN supplied the amino acid sequences, and other specialised models helped pick candidates. Of 322 minibinders tested, 35 (10.9%) bound their intended target: 5 hits for PD-L1, a protein some cancers use to evade the immune system, 3 for IL-7Rα, 1 for TrkA, 8 for VEGF-A and 18 for IL-17A. Every target got at least one hit. In separate experiments, many antibodies and minibinders that GPT-6.2 redesigned also bound. OpenAI says GPT-6.2’s designs scored slightly below the specialised RFdiffusion model on computer measures while its newer internal models scored higher, and that the original RFdiffusion study reported higher hit rates. It also says the results do not yet show end-to-end design without specialised models, that binding is only one step towards a medicine, and that the same skills could be misused.
stories.matters: General AI models are starting to do work that needed a chain of specialist tools and experts. For research teams that could mean trying ideas faster, but the lab, the filtering and the human judgment still decide what works.
stories.imply: Expect more “one general model plus a few specialist checks” workflows in science and engineering. Results like this need reading closely: who filtered the designs, how binding was defined, and who ran the lab.
uses: Biotech and research teams: compare a general model’s designs against your current specialist pipeline on one target you know well.
R&D managers: ask vendors what share of an AI-designed batch actually worked in the lab, not just computer scores.
Safety and compliance teams: review dual-use controls before giving staff biology-capable models.
stories.example: A university lab tests a general model on a protein target it has studied for years, sends 40 designs to its usual lab partner, and compares the hit rate with last year’s specialist-tool campaign.
stories.audience: Biotech researchers, R&D leaders and investors in drug discovery, and safety teams watching dual-use risk.
stories.watch: Independent replication, results from OpenAI’s internal models in the lab, and how labs govern access to protein-design abilities.

source.title: OpenAI: GPT-6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities, 24 November 2026
source.quote: We tested 322 minibinders against 5 targets in the lab. Of those, 35 (10.9%) tested positive for binding to their intended target.
